Privacy-focused search company DuckDuckGo recently released a new survey revealing how much personal information users share with AI chatbots, and how poorly the public understands where these conversations end up. Below are the survey details.

Survey shows AI users share more than they realize

DuckDuckGo published a survey today exploring various privacy issues related to AI chatbot usage. It noted that nearly one-third of users have told AI things they wouldn't share with friends, family, colleagues, or healthcare providers; among self-proclaimed AI enthusiasts, this figure rises to 56%.

Here's what DuckDuckGo says:

The company said that among approximately 2,000 U.S. adult respondents, 53% don't know or aren't sure that most chatbots default to using conversations for training purposes, and only 25% know that AI conversations can be subpoenaed by law enforcement.

The results also showed significant behavioral differences between parents and non-parents: parents or guardians living with their children confide in AI at nearly twice the rate of non-parents. DuckDuckGo noted that "among parents with children at home who use AI, 43% have told AI something they've never shared with anyone else," while "among AI users without children at home, that number drops to 25%."

DuckDuckGo believes that AI companies, through advertising and media exposure, encourage users to view chatbots as confidants, even though these conversations may not be as confidential as users believe.

Regarding trust, the survey found that the public has slightly more confidence in large AI companies than in the U.S. government's ability to protect their data. However, both are viewed with significant skepticism: 39% said they have no trust at all in large AI companies, while 48% feel the same about the government.

Finally, DuckDuckGo believes users still have the opportunity to change how they handle AI privacy, especially since chatbot usage habits are still emerging:

When we talk about online privacy with search engines and browsers, many people think, 'It's too late, my data has already been exposed.' But the most valuable information you can share with Big Tech is your next question—not the one you asked days, months, or even years ago. So it's never too late to switch to more privacy-focused online services.

The company also reminded users that they can take proactive steps to protect their privacy when using AI chatbots, including choosing services with clearer and more transparent data handling policies.
